stimulus.text: Excerpt 1: Historian Taylor Branch portrays Martin Luther King Jr. as the commanding figure of a national movement: King fused patriotism, ministry, and nonviolence; the movement seized the center of American politics in 1963, when President Johnson called segregation a moral issue; the Civil Rights Act of 1964 followed, King received the Nobel Peace Prize, and the 1965 Selma campaign produced the Voting Rights Act — a national moral crusade converting protest into federal law. (Paraphrased from Taylor Branch, At Canaan's Edge: America in the King Years, 1965–1968, 2006.) Excerpt 2: Historian Clayborne Carson argues local movements should not be seen merely as pressure campaigns on Washington. He describes constant tension between national leaders, who treated mass protest as an instrument for federal reform, and local organizers, who prioritized building enduring local institutions and forging new social identities for participants. Even where King played a major role — Albany, Birmingham, Selma — he had to work with local leaders reluctant to adopt outsiders' strategies, and the freedom struggle shows deep continuity across 1965. (Paraphrased from Clayborne Carson, 'Civil Rights Reform and the Black Freedom Struggle,' 1986.)

parts: Briefly describe ONE major difference between Branch's and Carson's historical interpretations of the American civil rights movement.
Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Branch's interpretation.
Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Carson's interpretation.
exemplar: Branch's interpretation centers on national leadership — especially King's — and federal legislation as the movement's engine and prize, while Carson's centers on local organizers whose goals (durable institutions, new collective identities) often diverged from the national leadership's protest-for-reform strategy.

The 1963 March on Washington — organized by national civil-rights leadership and culminating in King's 'I Have a Dream' speech — generated the political pressure that helped produce the Civil Rights Act of 1964, exactly the national-leader-driven, legislation-centered story Branch tells.

In the Albany Movement (1961–1962), SNCC field organizers resented King's SCLC 'parachuting in' with an outsider strategy; after King left, local activists regrouped around their own institution-building — the local-over-national tension Carson describes.

stimulus.text: "Since the peace was made [the 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne], you have kill'd some of the Shawanese, Winebagoes Delawares and Miamies and you have taken our lands from us and I do not see how we can remain at peace with you if you continue to do so. . . . We shall have a great council, at which all the tribes will be present, when we shall show to those who sold [land] that they had no right to [do so]. . . . If you will not give up the land and do cross the boundary of your present settlement, it will be very hard, and produce great troubles among us. . . . As we intend to hold our council at the Huron village, that is near the British, we may probably make them a visit. Should they offer us any presents of goods, we will not take them; but should they offer us powder and the tomahawk, we will take the powder and refuse the tomahawk." — Tecumseh, speech to Governor William Henry Harrison at Vincennes, Indiana Territory, 1810

parts: Briefly describe one likely purpose of Tecumseh in giving the speech.
Briefly explain how one historical development contributed to the circumstance discussed in the excerpt.
Briefly explain one development between 1810 and 1840 that resulted from situations such as the one depicted in the excerpt.
exemplar: Tecumseh aimed to convince Harrison that the Treaty of Fort Wayne was void — no single tribe's chiefs could sell land held in common — and to warn that if the United States kept seizing land, his united confederacy would resist by force and accept British military aid.

The 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne, in which Harrison secured some three million acres from Delaware, Miami, and Potawatomi signers, created the crisis: Tecumseh insisted those chiefs had no authority to sell shared tribal territory, so settler occupation under the treaty was, to him, theft.

The confrontation fed directly into the War of 1812, when Tecumseh allied his confederacy with Britain against the United States; his death at the Thames in 1813 shattered pan-Indian resistance in the Old Northwest and cleared the way for further American expansion.

stimulus.attribution: Described from the 1892 Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper cartoon 'The People's Party Convention - Delegates Who Were Not In It' (Library of Congress).
stimulus.text: The satirical cartoon, 'The People's Party Convention - Delegates Who Were Not In It,' mocks the new People's (Populist) Party: panels show a 'Mixed Delegation' of odd characters, a scheming 'Lobby Delegate,' and a snoozing figure captioned 'Away From the Excitement,' while a 'Farmers Alliance' man turns his back. The cartoon portrays the 1892 convention as a farce staged by cranks and opportunists rather than a serious political movement.

parts: Briefly describe ONE perspective about politics in the 1890s expressed in this image.
Briefly describe ONE specific historical development that led to the political development depicted in the cartoon.
Briefly explain ONE effect that the political development depicted in the cartoon had on the United States in the period 1891 to 1920.
exemplar: The cartoon expresses the political establishment's contemptuous view of Populism: the People's Party convention is portrayed as a farce - a 'mixed delegation' of cranks, lobbyists, and sleepers - implying the movement is unserious and unfit to govern.

The party grew out of agrarian revolt against Gilded Age political economy — farmers crushed by railroad freight rates, high tariffs, and gold-standard deflation organized through the Grange and the Farmers' Alliances, and the 1891 Cincinnati convention channeled that discontent into a third party.

Though the party itself faded, its Omaha Platform demands reshaped American politics: the graduated income tax and direct election of senators were enacted as the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Amendments in 1913, and railroad regulation became a core Progressive cause.
